articles.title: After 30 years of cultural revival, the Siraya reclaim their Indigenous status in Taiwan
articles.summary: The Indigenous Siraya were officially recognized via executive decree as Taiwan’s 17th indigenous group on July 30. They are also the first plains tribe group to obtain Indigenous status in Taiwan.
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Indigenous Siraya were officially recognized via executive decree as Taiwan’s 17th indigenous group on July 30. They are also the first plains tribe group to obtain Indigenous status after the passage of the Plains Indigenous Peoples Status Act in October 2025.

Like other Indigenous tribes in Taiwan, Siraya society was matriarchal, and its people, belonging to the Austronesian, spoke a distinctive language known as Sinckan, which was recorded through romanization by missionaries during the Dutch colonial era (1624–1662).

Siraya people settled in the southwestern plain areas of Taiwan’s main island long before the Qing Dynasty took over Dutch Formosa in 1683, when some of the tribes were forced to relocate to the southeastern coast.

The tribal group practiced Animism and had unique ritualistic practices to worship the spiritual interconnectedness of the human and natural world. However, their culture and language almost vanished as a result of more than three centuries of forced assimilation, first under the Qing dynasty, followed by Japanese imperial rule, and then military dictatorship under the Kuomintang (KMT) of the Republic of China (ROC).

It has taken more than 30 years for the Siraya to rediscover, reconstruct, and revive their language and culture. Below is a video showing one of the very few surviving matriarchal rituals:

Comparing the mountains and the plains Indigenous groups

Under Qing colonial rule (1684–1895), the Indigenous peoples in Taiwan were divided into two categories: The “raw” or “uncivilized barbarians” (生番), who resided in the mountainous areas and resisted the Qing administration, and the “mature” or “civilized barbarians” (熟番), who resided in the flatland, paid taxes, and submitted to the government. Siraya people were categorized as mature barbarians.

The Qing government forced them to abandon their mother tongue; submit to Manchu rulers by shaving their hair; learn the Chinese language; and adopt Han surnames, rituals, and culture.

During the Japanese colonial period (1895–1945), the Japanese administrators continued dividing the Austronesian Indigenous peoples into two major categories: First, the plains Indigenous or Pingpu (平埔) peoples, who, along with Han settlers, were considered natives; second, the mountain Indigenous or the Takasago peoples, which consisted of nine unique ethnic groups. The Pingpu and Takasago peoples were geographically segregated by a military line built by the Japanese for administrative purposes, with the mountainous regions placed under military control.

After the KMT, the ruling party of the Republic of China, fled to Taiwan from mainland China upon the defeat of the Chinese Civil War in 1949, it adopted Japan’s colonial division, distinguishing Indigenous groups as “mountain compatriots” (山胞) and Pingpu peoples. But only those living in mountainous areas were registered as Indigenous peoples, while Pingpu tribes were treated like ordinary Han.

Under KMT military dictatorship (1949–1987), through education, administrative measures, and public shaming, the Pingpu tribes were forced to assimilate into Han’s culture. On the other hand, the mountain regions were designated as “restricted zones” which required special permits to enter. Thus, the KMT maintained exclusive access to the tribal communities and established patronage relations with Indigenous elites through public appointment and business licenses to sustain their single-party dictatorship with manipulated local elections.

The KMT government began to legally register Aboriginal land in Taiwan as Aboriginal Reserve Land in 1968, which granted the Indigenous tribes user rights and restricted the selling of land to Han Chinese. However, legal loopholes resulted in land seizure by developers, corporations, and local governments. It was only after Taiwan began democratizing in the early 1990s that Indigenous peoples had the space to protest for their rights.

Indigenous rights movements since democratization

Since that democratization, waves of Indigenous rights movements emerged and brought series of substantial policy changes — the derogatory term “mountain compatriots” was replaced with “Indigenous peoples” in 1994, the mandatory Han surname registration system was dropped in 1995, a cabinet-level Council of Indigenous Peoples was established in 1996 to coordinate related affairs, the collective rights of the Indigenous were codified in 1997, and Indigenous peoples’ right to education was codified in 1998.

However, Pingpu descendants’ claim for Indigenous status had been deferred as their ancestral lands are flatlands with developmental potential. Some insisted that the Pingpu have been assimilated into Han Chinese through intermarriage, and some were worried that an influx of new Indigenous members would expand the pool of privileged citizens, as Indigenous peoples in Taiwan are entitled to reserved seats in the legislature, as well as social and educational benefits through affirmative action.

It was only in 2022, through a landmark Constitutional Court ruling, that the Indigenous rights of Pingpu were recognized, which was later codified in the 2025 Plains Indigenous People Status Act. The Siraya people are the first among Pingpu to have successfully claimed their Indigenous status — a journey that took more than 30 years.

Like other Pingpu tribes, Siraya’s struggle began with land rights, as they were excluded from registering their ancestral lands under the Aboriginal Reserve Land policy. Their protests later evolved into legal battles and cultural movements among the Pingpu Indigenous tribes, including Siraya.

Among the Siraya activists, the dedication of the Talavan family stands out, having devoted three generations to reviving Siraya’s culture and language. The first generation, 85-year-old Cheng-hiong Talavan, founded the Tainan Pepo Siraya Culture Association (TPSCA) in 1999 to reconstruct Siraya people’s historical legacy and preserve their culture through oral history and collection of relics. His daughter Uma Talavan and her husband Edgar Macapili, who is a member of the Bisaya Indigenous people in the Philippines, decoded the Sinckan language through word-by-word translation of a Sirayan translation of “The Gospel of St. Matthew” written by early Dutch missionaries into English, Dutch, and Bisayan (an Austronesian language similar to Sinckan). The couple managed to recover 4,000 Sinckan vocabulary words and used the language to write children’s books and educational songs. The third generation, Euphone and Lici Talavan, have devoted themselves to revitalizing Siraya culture and spreading awareness.

Below are five ancient Siraya songs performed by young learners:

One Talavan family member, under the username @miss5langs, highlighted the significance of the recognition of Siraya’s Indigenous status via a post on Threads:

西拉雅正名，不是為了把任何人排除在外，也不是為了製造對立，而是希望那些曾經被歷史遮蔽的名字，終於能夠重新被看見。 也希望更多人能因為這次正名，願意去了解臺灣這片土地真正的歷史，理解平埔族群曾經走過的道路，理解語言與文化為什麼會消失，也理解這些族人並不是突然出現，而是一直都在。 即使現在的我生活在國外，我仍然會很驕傲地告訴身邊的人：我是來自臺灣，我是西拉雅族。這不是為了任何福利，也不是為了任何標籤，而是因為，這一直都是我的名字。

The recognition of the Siraya’s Indigenous status is not intended to exclude anyone or create division, but rather to ensure that the names once obscured by history can finally be seen again. I also hope that, through this [identity] restoration, more people will be willing to learn about the true history of Taiwan, understand the paths the Pingpu peoples have walked, comprehend why their languages and cultures have disappeared, and realize that these peoples did not suddenly appear — they have always been here. Even though I now live abroad, I will still proudly tell those around me: I am from Taiwan, and I am Siraya. This is not for any benefits, nor is it for any label — it is simply because this has always been my name.

In addition to Siraya, Kavalan, Ketagalan, Taokas, Pazeh, Papora, Babuza, Hoanya, and Makatau groups are classified as Pingpu, and they are also working to apply for official recognition of their Indigenous status.

articles.personality_title: Taiwan’s Siraya people officially recognized as Indigenous after 30 years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Siraya are an Indigenous group from Taiwan’s southwestern plains. For hundreds of years, their culture and language nearly disappeared due to colonization and forced assimilation under different rulers, including the Qing dynasty, Japan, and Taiwan’s former government. 

**What happened** – On July 30, 2026, Taiwan officially recognized the Siraya as its 17th Indigenous group through an executive decree. This recognition followed the 2025 law called the Plains Indigenous Peoples Status Act and marks the first time a plains tribe has gained Indigenous status in Taiwan.

**Impact** – This recognition is important because it acknowledges the Siraya’s long history and their distinct culture, language, and rights. It corrects decades of exclusion, allowing them access to legal protections, cultural support, and political representation. The Siraya’s journey also highlights the success of decades-long efforts by families and activists who revived their language and traditions.

**What’s next step** – Other plains Indigenous groups like the Kavalan, Ketagalan, and Taokas are now working to gain official recognition too. The Siraya recognition may encourage more people to learn about Taiwan’s full Indigenous history and help protect the rights and cultures of all Indigenous peoples on the island.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After 30 years of cultural revival and legal struggle, Taiwan’s Siraya people have been officially recognized as Indigenous, marking a historic step for their community and others like them.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les Siraya de Taïwan officiellement reconnus comme peuple autochtone après 30 ans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Siraya sont un peuple autochtone des plaines du sud-ouest de Taïwan. Leur culture et leur langue ont presque disparu à cause de la colonisation et de l’assimilation forcée sous plusieurs gouvernements, dont la dynastie Qing, le Japon et l’ancien gouvernement taïwanais.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 30 juillet 2026, Taïwan a officiellement reconnu les Siraya comme son 17e groupe autochtone par décret exécutif. Cette reconnaissance fait suite à la loi de 2025 sur le statut des peuples autochtones des plaines, et c’est la première fois qu’une tribu des plaines obtient ce statut à Taïwan.

**Impact** – Cette reconnaissance est importante car elle reconnaît l’histoire, la culture, la langue et les droits distincts des Siraya. Elle corrige des décennies d’exclusion et leur donne accès à des protections légales, un soutien culturel et une représentation politique. Le parcours des Siraya montre aussi le succès d’efforts de plusieurs décennies menés par des familles et militants pour faire revivre leur culture.

**Prochaine étape** – D’autres peuples autochtones des plaines comme les Kavalan, Ketagalan et Taokas cherchent aussi à être officiellement reconnus. La reconnaissance des Siraya pourrait encourager plus de personnes à découvrir l’histoire complète des autochtones de Taïwan et aider à protéger les droits et cultures de tous les peuples autochtones de l’île.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après 30 ans de renaissance culturelle et de lutte juridique, les Siraya de Taïwan sont officiellement reconnus comme autochtones, une étape historique pour leur communauté et d’autres groupes similaires.
articles.personality_title_es: Los Siraya de Taiwán reconocidos oficialmente como indígenas tras 30 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los Siraya son un pueblo indígena de las llanuras del suroeste de Taiwán. Su cultura y lengua casi desaparecieron debido a la colonización y asimilación forzada bajo varios gobiernos, incluyendo la dinastía Qing, Japón y el antiguo gobierno de Taiwán.

**Qué pasó** – El 30 de julio de 2026, Taiwán reconoció oficialmente a los Siraya como su decimoséptimo grupo indígena mediante un decreto ejecutivo. Este reconocimiento siguió a la ley de 2025 sobre el estatus de los Pueblos Indígenas de las Llanuras, y es la primera vez que una tribu de las llanuras obtiene este estatus en Taiwán.

**Impacto** – Este reconocimiento es importante porque reconoce la larga historia, cultura, lengua y derechos únicos de los Siraya. Corrige décadas de exclusión y les da acceso a protecciones legales, apoyo cultural y representación política. El camino de los Siraya también muestra el éxito de décadas de esfuerzos de familias y activistas para revivir su cultura.

**Próximo paso** – Otros pueblos indígenas de las llanuras como los Kavalan, Ketagalan y Taokas también buscan el reconocimiento oficial. El reconocimiento de los Siraya puede motivar a más personas a aprender sobre la historia completa indígena de Taiwán y ayudar a proteger los derechos y culturas de todos los pueblos indígenas en la isla.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Tras 30 años de renacimiento cultural y lucha legal, los Siraya de Taiwán han sido oficialmente reconocidos como indígenas, un paso histórico para su comunidad y otras similares.

articles.title: UN continues scaling up response to earthquake in Colombia
articles.summary: The UN on Wednesday continued scaling up assistance to areas affected by the deadly earthquake that hit Colombia two days earlier.
articles.content:
Tweet URL

According to latest official figures, the 7.4 magnitude quake has left more than 200 dead and injured over 2,500, said UN Deputy Spokesperson Farhan Haq, briefing journalists in New York.

Homes and public infrastructure have also been severely damaged.

Humanitarian assessments are ongoing, particularly in the hardest-hit areas around Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo, where disruptions to communications, transport and public services continue to impede relief operations.

Children face ‘growing risks’

“Children have seen their homes and schools damaged and are facing growing risks as essential services remain disrupted in the hardest-hit communities,” said, UNICEF’s Country Representative, Tanya Chapuisat.

The top children’s agency official in the country said UNICEF was mobilising “an early response in Chocó and Buenaventura in water, sanitation and hygiene to help reduce public health risks and protect the dignity of affected families while essential services are being restored and assessments continue."

So far, the agency has reached 22,000 people in the Chocó and Buenaventura region along the Pacific coast – the epicentre of the quake – providing family hygiene kits, maternal care kits, menstrual kits and water storage tanks.

UNICEF has been active in the Chocó region for over two decades, so it is coordinating its response with national and local authorities and partners.

It is working with the Colombian Family Welfare Institute to strengthen child protection measures in the wake of the devastation.

© UNFPA

Cash and food assistance

Colombia was already facing a complex humanitarian crisis before Monday’s earthquake, due to continued conflict and climate shocks. Seven million people were already experiencing moderate or severe food insecurity in the country’s most vulnerable areas.

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has been active in Colombia for nearly six decades and has an established presence in some of the areas hit hardest by the earthquake.

Responding to the Government’s request for international assistance, the WFP is mobilising support and is ready to assist communities.

The organisation’s pre-existing cash-programme activities can help families meet urgent needs, and its 4,500 tonnes of pre-positioned food stocks in Colombia are ready to be dispatched if necessary.

“The stocks are located close enough to affected areas to enable a rapid response, with additional supplies available through WFP's regional and global supply networks,” said Deputy Country Director Giulia Baldi.

Communities fear further aftershocks, she added: “The first 72 hours after an earthquake are crucial for search and rescue, and for positioning food and relief supplies before needs escalate.”

Rescue teams are continuing to search through rubble in the hardest-hit cities, with people of all ages continuing to be dug out alive. “Every minute is vital,” the mayor of Cali said on Tuesday.

articles.personality_title: UN steps up aid after deadly earthquake in Colombia
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – On Monday, a strong earthquake with a magnitude of 7.4 struck Colombia, causing serious damage and affecting many communities. More than 200 people have died, and over 2,500 were injured. The quake damaged homes, schools, and public services, especially in cities like Cali, Pereira, Manizales, and Quibdo.

**What happened** – The United Nations (UN) quickly increased its help for those affected. UNICEF, the UN agency for children, is providing hygiene kits, clean water, and support for families in the hardest-hit areas like Chocó and Buenaventura. They are also working to protect children who lost their homes and schools. Meanwhile, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) is ready to deliver food and cash assistance using supplies already stored nearby.

**Impact** – This response is important because many people were already struggling with food shortages before the earthquake. The quick delivery of aid helps reduce health risks and supports families during a difficult time. Rescue teams continue searching for survivors, showing how urgent the situation is. The coordinated efforts by the UN and local authorities help reach thousands of people in need faster.

**What's next step** – Humanitarian groups will keep assessing damage and needs while restoring essential services like water and sanitation. They will continue providing food, health care, and protection for vulnerable groups, especially children. The UN plans to work closely with Colombian officials to strengthen support and prepare for any aftershocks.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN is rapidly providing food, water, and protection to thousands affected by Colombia’s earthquake, helping families recover and stay safe amid ongoing challenges.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU intensifie son aide après le tremblement de terre meurtrier en Colombie
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Lundi, un fort tremblement de terre de magnitude 7,4 a frappé la Colombie, causant de graves dégâts et touchant de nombreuses communautés. Plus de 200 personnes sont mortes et plus de 2 500 ont été blessées. Le séisme a endommagé des maisons, des écoles et des services publics, notamment dans des villes comme Cali, Pereira, Manizales et Quibdo.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les Nations Unies (ONU) ont rapidement renforcé leur aide aux personnes touchées. L’UNICEF, l’agence de l’ONU pour les enfants, fournit des kits d’hygiène, de l’eau potable et un soutien aux familles dans les zones les plus touchées comme Chocó et Buenaventura. Elle travaille aussi à protéger les enfants qui ont perdu leur maison et leur école. Le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) est prêt à distribuer nourriture et aides financières grâce à des stocks déjà stockés près des zones sinistrées.

**Impact** – Cette réponse est importante car beaucoup de personnes souffraient déjà de la faim avant le tremblement de terre. La livraison rapide de l’aide aide à réduire les risques sanitaires et soutient les familles en difficulté. Les équipes de secours continuent de chercher des survivants, montrant l’urgence de la situation. La coordination entre l’ONU et les autorités locales permet d’atteindre plus rapidement des milliers de personnes dans le besoin.

**Étape suivante** – Les groupes humanitaires continueront d’évaluer les dégâts et les besoins tout en rétablissant les services essentiels comme l’eau et l’assainissement. Ils poursuivront la distribution de nourriture, de soins de santé et la protection des groupes vulnérables, notamment les enfants. L’ONU prévoit de collaborer étroitement avec les autorités colombiennes pour renforcer le soutien et se préparer à d’éventuelles répliques.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’ONU apporte rapidement nourriture, eau et protection à des milliers de personnes touchées par le tremblement de terre en Colombie, aidant les familles à se remettre et à rester en sécurité malgré les défis.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU intensifica la ayuda tras el terremoto mortal en Colombia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El lunes, un fuerte terremoto de magnitud 7.4 sacudió Colombia, causando graves daños y afectando a muchas comunidades. Más de 200 personas murieron y más de 2,500 resultaron heridas. El sismo dañó casas, escuelas y servicios públicos, especialmente en ciudades como Cali, Pereira, Manizales y Quibdó.

**Qué pasó** – Las Naciones Unidas (ONU) aumentaron rápidamente su ayuda para los afectados. UNICEF, la agencia de la ONU para la infancia, está proporcionando kits de higiene, agua limpia y apoyo a las familias en las zonas más afectadas como Chocó y Buenaventura. También trabajan para proteger a los niños que perdieron sus hogares y escuelas. El Programa Mundial de Alimentos (PMA) está listo para entregar alimentos y asistencia en efectivo usando suministros almacenados cerca.

**Impacto** – Esta respuesta es importante porque muchas personas ya enfrentaban escasez de alimentos antes del terremoto. La entrega rápida de ayuda ayuda a reducir riesgos de salud y apoya a las familias en un momento difícil. Los equipos de rescate siguen buscando sobrevivientes, mostrando la urgencia de la situación. Los esfuerzos coordinados de la ONU y las autoridades locales ayudan a llegar más rápido a miles de personas necesitadas.

**Próximo paso** – Los grupos humanitarios continuarán evaluando daños y necesidades mientras restauran servicios esenciales como agua y saneamiento. Seguirán proporcionando alimentos, atención médica y protección para los grupos vulnerables, especialmente los niños. La ONU planea trabajar de cerca con las autoridades colombianas para fortalecer el apoyo y prepararse para posibles réplicas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La ONU está proporcionando rápidamente alimentos, agua y protección a miles afectados por el terremoto en Colombia, ayudando a las familias a recuperarse y mantenerse seguras ante los desafíos continuos.
